children: The Indian rupee opened 11 paise lower at 95.49 against the US dollar on Monday (August 31), compared with Friday’s (August 28's) close of 95.38, as a stronger dollar and elevated crude oil prices kept pressure on the domestic currency.
The rupee had gained 0.2% last week to end at 95.3775/$, but trading remained largely rangebound, with the currency moving within a narrow band of around 30 paise.
Why is the rupee under pressure?
One of the key concerns for the rupee is the growing possibility of a US Federal Reserve rate hike at its September 15-16 meeting.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said on Friday (August 28) that the central bank may need to raise interest rates if inflation remains above its 2% target. The comments led investors to sharply increase their bets on a September rate hike.

Market expectations for a hike rose to nearly 60%, from around 35% before Warsh's comments. A higher US interest rate outlook can support the dollar and reduce the appeal of emerging-market currencies such as the rupee.

Crude oil prices are another headwind. Brent crude moved back towards $90 a barrel on Monday. Higher oil prices are negative for the rupee because India imports most of its crude requirements, increasing demand for dollars to pay for those imports.
Despite these pressures, the rupee has remained relatively stable in recent weeks, partly because of regular intervention by the Reserve Bank of India.

Market participants remain cautious about taking large bets against the rupee, as the RBI is expected to intervene if the currency weakens sharply. At the same time, demand from importers looking to hedge future dollar payments has limited the rupee's gains.
The rupee is therefore expected to remain rangebound in the near term, although the broader bias remains towards depreciation.
The US economic calendar is also important, with manufacturing and services activity data, employment indicators and the August jobs report due ahead of the Fed's September meeting.

title: Rupee weakens 11 paise to 95.49 against dollar: What’s weighing on the currency
